data.content_ref: inline:The flock-of-birds analogy contains a self-undermining tension: it identifies that a flock's instinctual responses can be 'easily hijacked by a single predator cue' and that decentralized networks can be synchronized by endogenous shared signals (market prices), yet its shared-structure framing still treats the nominal independence of birds/nodes as the transferred basis for resilience. The very mechanism it highlights — a single cue collapsing many independent agents into correlated behavior — is evidence that apparent independence is not true independence, which is what the problem asks to distinguish; the analogy should undercut its own transfer claim more decisively rather than leaving the 'nominally independent agents' framing to carry the pro-decentralization side.
